extracted.intended_audience: Victorian magazine readers; writers of humorous sketches and social satire
extracted.subtask_description: Produce short, character-driven humorous sketches and satirical vignettes in the style of Victorian periodicals — focusing on social observation, comic characterisation, and pithy narration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public-performance readiness (biped lions)
rubrics_metrics.description: “these appear flattered by the attentions that are paid them; while those conceal themselves ... these court the popular eye, and, unlike their brethren, whom nothing short of compulsion will move to exertion, are ever ready to display their acquirements to the wondering throng.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A successful social celebrity/character in a sketch should court attention and seize display opportunities — be prepared to perform and show off acquirements whenever occasion offers. Portray eagerness for the popular eye as part of comic characterisation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of a foil/setup to land jokes
rubrics_metrics.description: “the latter takes all the up-hill work, and is content to pioneer to the jokes and repartees of Mr. P. himself, who never fails to gain great credit and excite much laughter thereby.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deploy a ‘keeper’ or foil who does the preparatory work (setups, leading remarks) so the principal comic figure can deliver the smart lines and reap the credit. This stage-model (one pioneers, the other shines) is recommended for social wit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Topical and concrete punning (table-based jokes)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Such flashes of wit as he elicited from the lion! First of all, they began to make puns upon a salt-cellar, and then upon the breast of a fowl, and then upon the trifle; but the best jokes of all were decidedly on the lobster salad, upon which latter subject the lion came out most vigorously, and, in the opinion of the most competent authorities, quite outshone himself.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use concrete, everyday objects and situations (food, table items) as springboards for puns and repartee. Building a running sequence of escalating jests around a visible scene helps a comic performance ‘outshine’ itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy and compression in sensational storytelling
rubrics_metrics.description: “The whole horrible ideality of the Mysteries of Udolpho, condensed into the pithy effect of a ten-line paragraph, could not possibly have so affected the narrator’s auditory.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For maximum comic or sensational effect, compress narrative: condense melodrama or mystery into a short, tightly-wrought paragraph with a vivid climax. Choose a few sharp details to imply a larger lurid scene rather than lengthy exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative stagecraft and timing
rubrics_metrics.description: Descriptions such as Bolton taking “a very long draught of porter, and some two or three dozen whiffs of tobacco” to set up his authority, and the use of pauses that drew “entire silence” as testimony to effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use physical gestures, deliberate pacing, and pauses in narration (or in performance) to control the audience’s reaction. Small stage actions and timed emphases (repetition of a shocking word, a long pause) heighten comedic or dramatic payoff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedic character description through contrast
rubrics_metrics.description: Mr. Bolton’s dress: “Half of him was dressed for the winter, the other half for the summer... his _tout ensemble_ was hidden beneath the enormous folds of an old brown poodle-collared great-coat.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create humour by juxtaposing mismatched or contradictory physical details (attire, deportment). Sharp, concrete contrasts in appearance and behaviour quickly produce comic effect and memorable characters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Irony and contrast in social satire
rubrics_metrics.description: “The lions of the fashionable world look just as ferocious, and are the most harmless creatures breathing.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Routinely contrast appearance with reality to satirise social types. Present pompous or fierce demeanour and then undercut it by showing harmlessness, vanity, or performative courage to produce ironic humour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Silence as dramatic applause
rubrics_metrics.description: “Silence, the purest and most noble of all kinds of applause, bore ample testimony to the barbarity of the baker, as well as to Bolton’s knack of narration.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognise and cultivate moments where deliberate silence (or the absence of immediate laughter) functions as the strongest audience response. Use it as a device to let a compressed or shocking image settle and achieve its effect.
